column6: Greaser, #88, throws sludge and hits bombs. She's also a decent mechanic.
column7: Throws sludge and hits bombs. Also a decent mechanic.

column5: Thickly built with a filthy, vile slider. It's so sick, even their catcher can't contain it
column6: The Princess of Putrid. The Goddess of Garbage. The Founder of Filth. The Duchess of Doom. The Mother of Mire. The Scum Slinger. The Nasty. The Vile. The Foul One. The grungiest, grittiest, gnarliest, gunslinger to ever grace the grounds. Your favorite villain, #89, Muck.
column7: Nasty. Vile. Foul. Putrid. Filthy. The grungiest gunslinger to ever grace the grounds.

column5: Its hard shell repels any kind of attack. It is vulnerable only when its shell is open
column6: Cup, #90, has Laggard's number. She makes sure his slow delivery bites him on the ass every chance she gets.
column7: Has Laggard's number. Makes sure that slow delivery bites him on the ass every time.

column5: When attacked, it launches its horns in quick volleys. Its innards have never been seen
column6: This is Dish, #91. She's known for shelling great pitchers and gunning down baserunners with frozen ropes from the warning track.
column7: Known for shelling great pitchers and gunning down runners with frozen ropes.

column5: Almost invisible, this gaseous PLAYER cloaks the target and puts it to sleep without notice
column6: Gas, #92, is a dead pull hitter.
column7: A dead pull hitter

column5: Because of its ability to slip through block walls, it is said to be from an- other dimension
column6: Mortimer, #93, walked out of a cornfield and onto the ball field one day, and he's been killin' it ever since.
column7: Walked out of a cornfield and onto the ball field one day. Been killin' it ever since.

column5: Under a full moon, this PLAYER likes to mimic the shadows of people and laugh at their fright
column6: Macobb, #94, is a nightmare to face. Throws a knuckleball that moves like it's possessed.
column7: A nightmare to face. Throws a knuckleball that moves like it's possessed.

column5: As it grows, the stone portions of its body harden to become similar to a diamond, but colored black
column6: This monolith of a man is Onyx, #95. He's the tallest player on the field by a whole lot and an excellent defensive first baseman. It's nearly impossible to throw it over his head, and he can reach half way across the diamond to grab a throw on close plays.
column7: Nearly impossible to throw over and can reach half way across the diamond.

column5: Puts enemies to sleep then eats their dreams. Occasionally gets sick from eating bad dreams
column6: Don't sleep on Zee, #96. He may not be a very athletic first baseman, but he's an incredible actor. At least a few times a game, he'll convince the runner on first that the ball got away from or that he's already thrown it back to the pitcher.
column7: Not a very athletic first baseman, but an incredible actor.

column5: When it locks eyes with an enemy, it will use a mix of PSI moves such as HYPNOSIS and CONFUSION
column6: Sooth, #97, is a master of the deke. His new found arm strength and recent move to the outfield has made runners' jobs much more difficult. They tag up on balls hit nowhere close to him, and get doubled up on when he pretends to lose the ball in the sun.
column7: Master of the deke. Tricks runners into getting doubled up.

column5: Its pincers are not only powerful weapons, they are used for balance when walking sideways
column6: He calls himself Rich. Everyone else calls him Dick, #98. He's one crabby player, but he sure can hit the ball hard. Just look at those forearms.
column7: Crabby PLAYER who can hit the ball hard.

column5: The large pitcher throws 100 mph and has crushing power. However, its huge size makes it unable to field
column6: Rex, #99, has crushing power to every corner of the field. It's too bad he keeps skipping leg day. Anything shy of a home run turns into a long single.
column7: Crushing power but skips leg day. Anything shy of a home run turns into a long single.

column5: Usually found in power plants. Easily mistaken for a # BALL, they have zapped many people
column6: There's plenty of room on this guy's jersey for that third digit. Don't let his size fool you, though. Speedball, #100,  is easily one of the fastest guys out there. It's like watching a ball of pure energy zipping around the field.
column7: One of the fastest guys out there. A ball of pure energy zipping around the field.

column5: It stores electric energy under very high pressure. It often explodes with little or no provocation
column6: When Tucker, #101, stopped swinging from the right and started laying down bunts from the left, his batting average doubled. This man has some explosive speed.
column7: Started bunting from the left and doubled their batting average. Explosive speed.

column5: Often mistaken for a group of people. A disturbed, one-armed man with lots of tattoos of himself.
column6: Ed, #102, lost an arm in a prison game when he tried to rob a homer and got it caught in the razor wire. The ball stayed in his glove, but the ump ruled it a home run since the arm was no longer attached to the player.
column7: Lost an arm robbing a home run in a prison game. Covered in tattoos of himself.

column5: His other arm miraculously grew back. Legend has it, the arm he lost grew a human, too.
column6: Edd, #103, found religion when he got out. He got clean, grew his arm back, and started hitting dingers. #Blessed
column7: Found religion, got clean, grew his arm back, and started hitting dingers.

column5: Because it never removes its giant hat, no one has ever seen this PLAYER's real face
column6: Bones, #104, lost her mother in a tragic hit and run accident. She called for a pitchout, and the batter tried to hit it anyway. The only thing she has left of her mother's is a hat that's still a bit too large on her.
column7: Lost their mom in a tragic accident. Wears their mom's hat, but it's still too big.

column5: Thier bat is the key to their success. They often throw their bat skillfully like a boomerang make contact with the ball.
column6: Marrow, #105, looks and plays just like her mother. She's aggressive behind the plate, aggressive at the plate, and aggressive on the basepaths until she touches the plate. Mom would be proud.
column7: Looks and plays just like mom behind, at, and stepping on the plate.

column5: When in a hurry, its legs lengthen progressively. It runs smoothly with extra long, loping strides
column6: Bruce, #106, generates all of his power from his legs. He has a high kick that hides the ball well, but it also causes him to be a bit wild. He often sails the ball over the batter's head.
column7: Generates power from his legs. High kick hides the ball well, but a bit wild.

column5: While apparently doing nothing, it fires punches in lightning fast volleys that are impossible to see
column6: Jackie, #107, packs a powerful punch at the plate. She's a contact hitter who can slap the ball anywhere there's a gap, but, if a pitcher lets their guard down, she'll gladly knock it out of the park.
column7: Packs a powerful punch. Contact hitter who can slap the ball anywhere.

column5: Its tongue can be extended like a chameleon's. It leaves a tingling sensation when it licks enemies
column6: It's unclear whether Lick, #108, got their nickname from how hard they hit the ball or how often they put their tongue on the bat.
column7: Unclear if their name came from how hard they hit the ball or how often they lick the bat.

column5: Because they inhale several kinds of toxic gases, they're prone to explosive diarrhea.
column6: When asked if he would consider giving up smoking, at least on the field, to set a better example to children, Ash, #109, responded, "I am a child. Why don't you ask why they keep selling cigarettes to a 12-year-old?"
column7: For a child, that's an awful lot of beard hair and cigarette smoke.

column5: When the cancer sets in, 2 ASHes can fuse into a SMOKEY over many years of surgery
column6: Smokey, #110, has the heart and lungs of a younger man, literally. Dude really needs to quit smoking and start eating healthier.
column7: Has the heart and lungs of a younger man, literally. Needs to quit smoking.

column5: Its massive bones are 1000 times harder than human bones. It can easily knock a trailer flying
column6: Rhino, #111, charges even hard-hit ground balls. He's a bit thick, but he's well liked because of how hard he plays the game.
column7: Charges every grounder. A bit thick, but liked because of how hard they play.

column5: Protected by an armor-like hide, it is capable of living in molten lava of 3,600 degrees
column6: Meet The Don, #112. He's a hard-nosed player and he still does his own dirty work. Stealing signs, doctoring the ball, sliding way out of the basepath to breakup plays, leaning into pitches, and paying off umpires are his specialties.
column7: Hard-nosed player who does his own dirty work.

column5: Genuinely cool. The kind of PLAYER everyone wants on their TEAM. Can't hit or field the ball.
column6: Chance, #113, is just the sweetest, happiest person on the field. They may not have overpowering stuff, but they're consistent, and they can go the distance. Whenever they start to feel tired, they eat a soft-boiled egg, and they're ready to get back on the mound.
column7: Sweetest, happiest person on the field. Consistent pitcher who can go the distance.

column5: Their whole body stinks of sea salt and weed. Their beards shake as they walk.
column6: Frizz, #114, was first scouted at a pickup game after a jam band festival. He's best known for his Kudzuball, a fastball with an unpredictable late break to it.
column7: Found at a pickup game after a jam band festival. Best known for their Kudzuball.

column5: Wears a protective pouch around her perpetually pregnant belly.
column6: After missing a season due to pregnancy, Gengis, #115, designed protective gear for pregnant women so no one else would ever have to choose between their career and and pregnancy again. She hasn't missed a season since, and she has enough kids for a league of their own.
column7: Designed gear for pregnant PLAYERS. Has enough kids for a league of her own.

column5: Known to down batters with precision pitches from the mound
column6: Brain, #116, has a baseball IQ of 1000. He's also really into marine biology, taxonomy, Greek mythology, neurology, and the grounds of schools with hippopotamuses for mascots.
column7: Baseball IQ over 9000. Into marine bio, neurology, Greek myths, and the grounds of schools with hippo mascots.

column5: Capable of throwing backwards by rapidly swinging their wing-like arms and stout legs
column6: This is Einstein, #117. My boy's wicked smart.
column7: Baseball IQ over 9000. They're wicked smart.

column5: Their golden locks billow like an elegant ballroom dress, giving them the nickname of the Dancing Queen
column6: Goldie, #118, at bat: This swing is too early. This swing is too late. This swing is just right.
column7: That swing is too early. That swing is too late. This swing is just right.

column5: In the post-season, they can be seen swimming powerfully up rivers and creeks to train
column6: She looks at changes out of the zone. She looks at splitters that fall off the table. She tries to find one to drive for the 50 million watching on cable. They call her The Seeker, #119. She takes low and high. Only swings if she gets what she's after, and it'll be a deep fly.
column7: Takes low and high. Only swings if she gets what she's after.

column5: An enigmatic PLAYER that can effortlessly generate a cheering crowd even when losing
column6: Starchild, #120, is adored by fans everywhere. He always puts on a show, and he's happy to stay as late as it takes to make sure every ball gets signed.
column7: Adored by fans everywhere. Always puts on a show and stays late to sign every ball.

column5: A core figure on any roster with a glow like the seven colors of the rainbow. Some fans value their personality above their skill
column6: People say that Starman, #121, is from another planet. Every one of his plate appearances and every ball hit his way brings the crowd to their feet in hopes of seeing something miraculous.
column7: Said to be from another planet. Brings the crowd to their feet on every play.

column5: Able to mirror every movement on the field. Knows where the ball is going before the pitcher.
column6: This is a Mime, #122. He's a decent ballplayer, but he never calls the ball, and sometimes he gets stuck in the batters box. The invisible rope trick that allows him to climb way up in the air to catch would-be home runs is pretty swell, though.
column7: Has a hard time leaving the box. Uses an invisible rope trick to rob home runs.

column5: With ninja-like agility and speed, they look like they're playing more than one position.
column6: Scy, #123, almost exclusively throws a cutter. Everyone knows it's coming, but it doesn't help much.
column7: Almost exclusively throws a cutter. Everyone knows it's coming, but it doesn't help.

column5: The seductive wiggle in their hips as they pitch can cause batters to forget to swing.
column6: Jinx, #124, has a knack for throwing off opposing players. When she puts the ball in play, there's a dramatic rise in throwing and fielding errors. On more than one occasion, I've seen on-target throws sail right past the first baseman without them even attempting to catch it.
column7: Has a knack for distraction. Hard to get them out when you're not watching the ball.

column5: Normally found near power plants, the static discharge of their swing can cause major blackouts in cities
column6: Buzz, #125, is an electric hitter with some serious power.
column7: An electric hitter with some serious power.

column5: Their heater always burns with an orange glow that enables it to hide perfectly among the lights of a scoreboard.
column6: Magma, #126, is a fire-breathing, face-melting, flamethrower.
column7: A fire-breathing, face-melting flamethrower.

column5: When they fail to crush the ball, they break their bat over their head.
column6: This is Pinch, #127. His grip strength is incredible.
column7: Incredible grip strength. Breaks his bat over his head when he fails to crush the ball.

column5: When hit by a pitch, they charge the mound and whip the pitcher with their long arms.
column6: Bull, #128, sees red and charges the mound when he gets hit by a pitch. Steer clear of him if you don't want beef.
column7: Sees red and charges the mound when hit. If you don't want beef, steer clear.

column5: Their parents played ball well, but these PLAYERs clearly didn't get the BéiSBOL gene.
column6: Fish, #129, is exceptionally bad. He's never been on base, and he's never recorded an out, but you have to admire the determination and mental fortitude it takes to keep showing up and trying.
column7: Exceptionally bad. Never been on base. Never made an out. Never stops trying.

column5: Rarely seen in the wild. Huge, vicious, and capable of knocking the cover off a ball.
column6: Gar, #130, is proof that with enough hard work, determination, and pent up rage from years of verbal abuse, anything is possible. His first hit went 500 ft. His first putout was immediately followed by a 350 ft. throw home for an assist. It's all been uphill from there.
column7: Proof that hard work and rage make anything possible. Huge hits and huge arm.

column5: A PLAYER that has been over- scouted almost to extinction. It can carry a team.
column6: What do you call someone who carries a team? The Bus, #131. She's an incredibly patient hitter with a great eye, and she's an expert at icing the pitcher. When you need to get a rally started, she's the stone-cold hitter who gets it done.
column7: Incredibly patient hitter with a great eye. Expert at icing the pitcher.

column5: Capable of copying an opponents's style to instantly transform themselves into a duplicate of the opponent.
column6: Yeah-Yeah, #132, tries hard to be like everyone else. On the mound or in the box, he does his best to mimic the windups and stances of those he's just faced, but he can't get the subtleties of human interaction right. The blank stare and forced smile is the best he can do.
column7: Tries hard to fit in. Mimics windups and stances of opponents.

column5: Their future is wide open. They can grow up to be anything they want to be.
column6: Evie, #133, hasn't yet decided what she wants to be when she grows up, but I'm sure it will be something special. She also asked me to let y'all know that her name starts with a short E sound, like "evolution".
column7: Hasn't decided what she wants to be when she grows up, but it will be something special.

column5: Lives at the beach. They go on long swims in the deep ocean and are often mistaken for mermaids
column6: Vapor, #134, is a finesse hitter with a surprising amount of power. He's also a licensed marine veterinarian who volunteers at the local aquarium on his off days. He loves narwhals, manatees, and doubling into the gap.
column7: Licensed marine veterinarian who loves hitting doubles in the gap.

column5: They accumulate negative ions in their hair. It gives a little extra zip to their throws.
column6: Jolt, #135, is a speedy middle infielder with some zip to their arm. They're also a card carrying member of the electrical workers union, a labor organizer, and a hobbyist retro console modder.
column7: Union electrician. Labor organizer. Hobbyist console modder. Speedy middle infielder.

column5: In the moments before each pitch, they get an adrenaline rush.
column6: Flare, #136, is a hard throwing, hard hitting corner outfielder with a fiery attitude. She's also an accomplished author, illustrator, and programmer of interactive children's books.
column7: Fiery outfielder. Author and programmer of interactive children's books.

column5: A PLAYER who spends a lot of time writing code. They often run the team website and keep stats.
column6: Polygon, #137, is a data nerd. He records all of the games, keeps the books, runs the team website, and crunches the numbers. If there's a pattern that can be found, it can be fixed or exploited. He's the least athletic guy on the team, but, arguably, the most valuable.
column7: Data nerd. Keeps the books. Crunches numbers. Least athletic. Most valuable.

column5: Although long retired, in rare cases, these early pioneers of batting helmets will play ball.
column6: Spiral, #138, is a fossil, a relic of the small ball era, but, thanks to the de-aging techniques of modern science, he's getting a new lease on life. Too bad it doesn't work on hair.
column7: A relic of the small ball era getting a new lease on life.

column5: A deadball era PLAYER that retired when the heavy gear made it impossible to catch a wild pitch
column6: Spire, #139, is thoroughly enjoying his second prime, and he's making sure this one lasts longer. He eats healthier, exercises regularly, and he's finally embracing all that technology he'd been ignoring for decades.
column7: Enjoying a second prime. Eats healthy. Regular exercise. Loves modern tech.

column5: A PLAYER that was resurrected from a grave in what was once Elysian Fields.
column6: Cap, #140, missed out on youth baseball. He was too busy working. Now that he's retired and revitalized, he's finally getting a chance to play.
column7: Missed out on youth ball. Retired and revitalized. Finally playing.

column5: Their sleek shape is perfect for pitching. They strike out batters with a sharp curve and a fluid windup.
column6: Topper, #141, is having the time of his life. Baseball brings him the same competitive rush that the business world once did with significantly less risk.
column7: Baseball gives the same competitive rush capitalism once gave them.

column5: A relic of early BéiSBOL when pitchers would throw at your temple if you crowded the plate.
column6: Bonehead, #142, worked at a tar and rosin factory before safety standards existed. An unfortunate step left him encased in an amber tomb, and a century of scientific progress freed him to play baseball. The factory sends him free pine tar and rosin bags.
column7: Factory worker encased in amber for a century. Gets free pine tar and rosin bags.

column5: Lazy bums just eat and sleep. As their rotund bulk builds, they become steadily more slothful
column6: Bear, #143, is the real deal. He's one of the fastest guys out there. He can hit for contact and power. He throws laser beams. On a big frame like his, that takes lots of energy, so he's always eating or napping in the dugout.
column7: Real deal. Fast. Hits for contact and power. Throws lasers. Always eating or napping.

column5: A legendary PLAYER. They're said to appear to doomed batters who are in a  slump
column6: Art, #144, once pitched an immaculate game (81 pitches, 27 strikeouts). He was blackballed from Béisbol after refusing to be traded, so started his own team and barnstormed the countryside. Last I heard, he retired up north and makes toys.
column7: Pitched the only immaculate game. Refused to be traded. Retired up north. Makes toys.

column5: A legendary PLAYER. They're said to appear from the mist while dropping enormous lightning bolts to center
column6: He was a natural. A child showing up pros until an accident left him paralyzed. For decades, his name faded into obscurity... Game 7, bottom 9, 2 down, 2 on, 2 outs. Home team sends in an old man to pinch hit. Zaph, #145, digs in. The pitch. A thunderous sound. Lights out.
column7: A natural. Kid showed up pros until an accident paralyzed them for decades.

column5: Known as legendary fireballers. Every pitch creates a dazzling flash of flames
column6: Fenix, #146, was an ace, but she was told 82 won't cut it at the next level. She moved to short and made dazzling plays, but they needed a bat. Hit over .400, they say she's not fast enough. Leads in stolen bases, not enough power. Now she practices law.
column7: The greatest player to never get a chance to play. Quit to practice law.

column5: Long considered a mythical PLAYER until recently when a small barnstorming team was found playing in a remote field.
column6: Drats, #147, is from an island where they play baseball with bottle caps and broomsticks. Needless to say, he's really good at hitting curveballs.
column7: From an island where they play with bottle caps and broomsticks. Crushes curves.

column5: A mystical PLAYER that exudes a gentle aura. Good weather seems to follow them everywhere.
column6: Aire, #148, is the Prince of Pop. His greatest hits include the sound a glove makes when he throws a fastball, the sound of weak contact on his change, and the sound of the crowd when he shuts out the visiting team.
column7: Prince of Pop. Listen to the sounds of glove pop, bat crack, and crowd roar.

column5: An extremely rarely seen island PLAYER. Their BéiSBOL knowledge is said to belong in a higher league.
column6: Dragon, #149, gives back to the community he came from every chance he gets. Every school on his island has a proper baseball field, an updated computer lab and library, and free lunches now. He also makes time to play vitilla with the kids when he visits his home town.
column7: Gives back to his home island community. Plays vitilla with local kids.

column5: MIKE was created by a scientist after years of horrific gene splicing and DNA engineering experiments
column6: Mike, #150, was genetically engineered and trained from birth to destroy Béisbol's most sacred records. He's the strongest, fastest, smartest, most disciplined player to ever play the game.
column7: Genetically engineered to destroy records. Fastest, smartest, strongest ever.

column5: Some claim they're still barnstorming the countryside. Only a few left can say they saw them in LEAGUE play.
column6: Mick, #151, set records that most folks think will never be broken. He was the greatest player in the game. Then, one day, he just walked off the diamond, and no one ever saw him again.
column7: The greatest of all time. Still holds every batting record. Last seen barnstorming the countryside.
